lines.text: Earns 17% a year on all the money it uses
lines.why: For every ₹100 of shareholders' money and loans in the business, it made ₹17 of operating profit last year (better than 48% of Auto & auto components). Past years: very uneven; recent trend improving. Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 15, weak < 10 (default rule, all sectors).

lines.text: Keeps ₹14 of every ₹100 of sales as operating profit
lines.why: Operating margin 13.8% (better than 70% of Auto & auto components). Past years: up and down; recent trend flat. Colour from close peers (Auto Parts (Automobile and Auto Components), 34 stocks): middle half 5.33–13.5 (band rule PROXY).
For every ₹100 of shareholders' money, it has borrowed ₹10 (better than 69% of Auto & auto components). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≤ 0.5, weak > 1 (default rule, all sectors).

For every ₹100 of reported profit in recent years, ₹337 actually came in as cash (better than 95% of Auto & auto components). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 0.8, weak < 0.5 (default rule, all sectors).
₹100 of sales 3 years ago is about ₹164 now (better than 73% of Auto & auto components). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 10, weak < 0 (default rule, all sectors).

valuation.text: Price tag: cheaper than its close peers
valuation.why: The whole business costs 4× its yearly operating cash profit (EBITDA). Colour from close peers (Auto Parts (Automobile and Auto Components), 34 stocks): middle half 8.62–15.2 (band rule PROXY).

flags.text: Check: the accounts resemble past earnings-manipulation cases (Beneish M-score)
flags.why: M-score -0.99 is above the −1.78 line. This is a statistical hint, not proof, and the score is not yet validated on Indian companies: read the annual report's notes on receivables, margins and cash flow before trusting the profits.

flags.text: Thinly traded – hard to buy or sell without moving the price
flags.why: Typical day: about ₹0.9 crore traded (we exclude below ₹5 crore).

lenses.sp: Wants a large, steady, cheap company with a strong balance sheet.
lenses.vd: In Benjamin Graham's spirit: would probably pass.

ch.r: Market value above ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Graham avoided small companies; ₹5,000 crore is our Indian translation of 'adequate size'.

ch.r: Current assets ÷ current liabilities ≥ 2
ch.w: For every ₹100 it owes within a year, it holds ₹179 of cash, stock and dues coming in.

ch.r: Long-term debt ≤ current assets − current liabilities
ch.v: Long-term debt ₹19 cr vs working capital ₹79 cr
ch.w: Graham wanted the short-term cushion alone to be able to repay long-term loans.

ch.n: A profit every year for 10 years
ch.r: Positive earnings in each of the last 10 years
ch.w: A loss year already breaks this rule, whatever the other years show.

ch.r: Dividends every year for 20 years (India: 10 years)
ch.w: A gap of about 90 months without a dividend (2016-11 to 2024-05).

ch.n: Earnings per share up a third in 10 years
ch.r: EPS +33% over 10 years
ch.w: Not enough EPS history.

ch.r: PE ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
ch.w: You pay ₹18 for every ₹1 of average yearly profit over the last 3 yrs.
You pay ₹1.16 for every ₹1 of net worth.

ch.r: Price < √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share)
ch.w: With EPS ₹24.2 and book value ₹168 per share, Graham's ceiling price is ₹303.

ch.r: No loss in 10 years
ch.w: A loss year breaks the rule.

ch.n: Doesn't eat its cash in capex

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have

ch.r: Candid, sensible with capital, no governance red flags

ch.r: Share count not higher than last year

ch.r: Sales ÷ assets higher than last year
